idiom_name: asyncio.wait_for / asyncio.timeout around the queue receive (TimeoutError as the absence alarm)
implementation_notes: The blocking receive makes the pattern local: awaiting queue.get() inside asyncio.wait_for(...) - or asyncio.timeout() on Python 3.11+, which raises TimeoutError from a context manager - turns 'nothing arrived within the budget' into an ordinary exception, so the monitor needs no scheduled sweep and no last-seen bookkeeping beyond reporting. The arrival path is simply the successful branch, which restarts the budget. In thread/process-based stacks the same role is played by threading.Timer (one-shot, re-armed per arrival) or a monotonic stamp checked by a periodic sweep; and because an in-process watcher dies with the process, the escalation usually reports to something outside it (a metrics registry, a heartbeat ping to an external check service).
pitfalls: asyncio.wait_for cancels the awaited operation on timeout: wrapping more than the receive (e.g. receive plus processing) can drop a message that was handed over before cancellation - keep the timeout around queue.get() only.

Blocking stdlib calls (time.sleep, requests, database drivers) inside the watcher coroutine stall the whole event loop and make the watchman miss other subjects' deadlines; use asyncio primitives or asyncio.to_thread.

threading.Timer is one-shot: forgetting to re-arm it after each arrival silently disables the watchman with no error at all (a monitor that reports health by being silent) - prefer a monotonic stamp plus one periodic check.
time.monotonic() must stamp last-seen; time.time() is wall-clock and can move backwards, producing negative silence or alarms that never fire.
An asyncio task created without a strong reference can be garbage-collected mid-flight: keep the monitor task referenced (or run it under asyncio.TaskGroup) or the watchman disappears silently.

On Python 3.8-3.10 asyncio.wait_for raises asyncio.TimeoutError, which only became an alias of the builtin TimeoutError in 3.11: an except TimeoutError around the receive lets the timeout escape on older runtimes and kills the monitor task instead of alerting, so except asyncio.TimeoutError is the portable spelling.

variants.name: Threading/process stack with a re-armed one-shot timer
variants.idiom_name: threading.Timer re-armed on arrival + time.monotonic() stamp
variants.implementation_notes: For consumers that are threads or separate processes (socket servers, Celery workers, os.fork-based daemons): keep a monotonic last-seen stamp behind a lock and either re-arm a threading.Timer on every arrival or let one sweep thread compare stamps. Timer objects are one-shot and daemon threads die at interpreter exit, so the stamp, not the timer, is the durable state.
pitfalls: Daemon threads are killed at interpreter exit without running finally blocks, so an alert in flight can be lost exactly during a shutdown that is itself worth alarming about.
A sweep thread holding the lock while alerting serialises every arrival path behind a slow notifier.
